extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television viewers, and prospective contestants interested in the Star Search format
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, scoring methods, categories, and advancement mechanics used across versions of the television talent competition Star Search. Covers how acts were classified, judged (studio and at-home), advanced, and awarded in different eras (1983–1995, 2003–2004, 2026 reboot notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition categories (1983–1995 core list)
rubrics_metrics.description: While categories varied slightly from season to season, the ten basic categories during the 1983–1995 version were: Female singer; Male singer; Junior singer (Second half of the season); Teen singer (First half of the season); Group vocal; Dance; Junior dance (First half of the season); Teen dance (Second half of the season); Spokesmodel; Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts competed within these defined genre categories; category membership determined which other acts they would face and which prizes were eligible. The page lists how categories could shift by season (e.g., junior/teen splits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of categories contested per show
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight categories were contested per show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each episode featured competitions in eight of the available categories, meaning not every category necessarily appeared every episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection via auditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential contestants auditioned to be on the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts had to pass auditions to be selected as contestants; selection was a prerequisite to appearing in the head-to-head matchups shown on the broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head-to-head match format (champion vs. challenger)
rubrics_metrics.description: In each category, two selected contestants would compete, a champion and a challenger. The challenger would usually perform first, while the champion performed second. In later seasons, the champion performed first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance order could vary by season; one-on-one matches determined episode winners who could continue to defend a title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio judge scoring (1983–1995)
rubrics_metrics.description: All acts were judged by a panel of four judges, and each judge could award an act from one to four stars (later changed to five stars). Once both acts were complete, Ed would reveal the scores, and the best average won.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring was numerical (stars) from each judge, averaged across judges to determine the match winner. The numeric star scale changed over time (initially 1–4, later 1–5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio tie-break: audience vote (1983–1995)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there was a tie, a studio audience vote broke the tie, in which case the results were revealed at the end of the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ties after averaging judge scores were resolved by in-studio audience votes rather than further judge deliberation; results could be withheld until the episode's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancement by consecutive wins / retirement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Any performer must win at least several shows in a row, depending on the number of shows left in the season, to earn an entry into the next round of the competition; usually this was three or four wins in a row. In later seasons, three-match winners were automatically retired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advancement to later rounds depended on streaks of episode wins; later seasons capped champion runs by retiring three-match winners (automatic retirement) rather than allowing indefinite title defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semifinal procedure (most seasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most seasons, two semifinal shows took place, one in the fall, the other in the spring, prior to the championship show. Each semifinal used seven judges. No scoring was used, and the judges' votes weren't revealed, but the acts that won their semifinals would then compete in the championship show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semifinals relied on judge votes (seven judges) without publicly revealed numeric scores; selection of semifinal winners was by undisclosed judge voting rather than quantified scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Championship prizes and contract rules (1983–1995)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the championship show, winners of Male Vocalist, Female Vocalist, Vocal Group, Comedy, and Dance, were awarded $100,000 but no record contract was guaranteed. The winner of the Spokesmodel category was awarded $100,000 and a contract with a well-known modeling agency. Winners of Junior Vocalist, Junior Dance, Teen Vocalist, and Teen Dance won $10,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize amounts and ancillary awards (like modeling contracts) varied by category; monetary awards did not necessarily include industry deals such as record contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival studio and at-home combined scoring (2003–2004)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the first three seasons [2003–2004 revival], the three house judges, along with the one celebrity judge, gave each contestant a score on a scale from one to five stars, making a maximum studio score 20 stars. During each commercial break, the home audience went to www.cbs.com/star to rate the competitors who just performed. Each performer could earn up to another 20 stars from the home audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final results combined studio judge scores (max 20) and at-home audience scores (max 20) for a possible combined maximum; at-home voting during the broadcast affected match outcomes in addition to studio judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival tie-breaking and rounding rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If the score was tied, then Hall would read off each performer's score rounded to the nearest hundredth (the at-home score was initially rounded down to the nearest star, unless there was a tie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounding conventions for at-home scores (initially rounded down to nearest star) and final tie-resolution by precise decimal display were used to distinguish close outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival semifinal variation (three competitors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only real exception to this format during the first three seasons was that three people competed in the semi-final rounds, not two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semi-final round format in the revival sometimes featured three-way contests rather than two-person matches, changing the head-to-head dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battle of the Best / special returnee formats
rubrics_metrics.description: After the first three seasons, a special, 'Battle of the Best' show took place, where the three Adult Singer, Junior Singer, Comedian, and two Young Dancer Grand Champions were brought back to face off for an additional $100,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special episodes could reintroduce past champions/grand champions into further competition for additional prizes; formats for these specials deviated from regular match rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner's Circle mechanics (revival fourth season)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the fourth and final season [revival], three contestants in Adult Singer, Junior Singer, and Dance were brought back to initially compete. The show scrapped the celebrity judge and had three house judges for the entire series: Naomi Judd, MC Lyte, and Matti Leshem. With only three judges, a score of 15 stars was possible, and ties were broken by a majority vote between the three. Initially, in each category, three performers made up the 'Winner's Circle'. The winning challenger then had the chance to challenge one of the three performers in his or her respective Winner's Circle. The Winner's Circle performer then had to beat or tie the bar set by the challenger; ties were automatically given to the Winner's Circle performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This format combined a small fixed panel (3 judges, max 15 stars) with a persistent 'Winner's Circle' of incumbents; challengers could displace incumbents but ties favored incumbents, and majority votes resolved ties when numeric equality occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free pass and final-show judging constraints (revival)
rubrics_metrics.description: Halfway through the program, the three performers in each Winner's Circle competed against each other in a special show. The winner in each category not only received a trip home, but a free pass to the final show. In the final show, the three people in each Winner's Circle competed against each other for $100,000, but the judges were only allowed to give opinions and not allowed to score. This, along with the Free Pass show, were the only two shows which re-adopted the at-home voting concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain shows removed numeric scoring from judges (opinions only) and relied on at-home voting or other mechanisms to decide advancement; the 'free pass' altered who could be challenged going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit judge behavior and category-specific scoring tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A noted anecdote: Naomi gave many comics only one star in the revival (jokingly cited as a reason the Comedy category was scrapped in a season).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge behavior, biases, or scoring tendencies could materially affect outcomes and even category viability (e.g., comedic acts receiving consistently low scores influenced format decisions).
